question.text: When a person travels horizontally at 3 km/h, raindrops seem to descend straight vertically downwards. If the person speeds up to 6 km/h in the same direction, the falling rain appears to strike at an angle of 45° relative to the vertical. Determine the true speed of the rain.
conditions: apparent velocity of rain is vertical when man's speed is 3 km/h
apparent velocity of rain makes an angle of 45° with the vertical when man's speed is 6 km/h

figure.description: A standard 2D Cartesian coordinate system with the horizontal axis directed to the right labeled with unit vector î and the vertical axis pointing upward labeled with unit vector ĵ.

solution.approach: Write the rain's true velocity in horizontal and vertical parts, use the first condition to fix the horizontal part, then the second condition to fix the vertical part.

steps.text: Let the rain's true velocity have horizontal part v_x and vertical part v_y (downward). At 3 km/h the rain appears vertical, so the man's speed cancels the horizontal part of the rain.
At 6 km/h the rain appears at 45° to the vertical, so the horizontal and vertical parts of the relative velocity are equal in size.
The speed of the rain is the size of its full velocity vector.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the rain's horizontal speed as 6 km/h instead of 3 km/h, using the second walking speed instead of the first, gives a wrong vertical speed.
